title: Lesson 4: Being Courteous Even When You Disagree
summary: Professionalism does not require everyone to agree. It requires respectful listening, firm but polite language, and focus on the issue rather than the person.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Respectful disagreement, emotional control and professional communication

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine two therapists discussing how treatment rooms should be prepared before appointments.
One believes that preparing the room immediately after each session is the most efficient approach. The other believes preparation should follow a different sequence.
Both employees have reasons for their opinions.
The discussion begins calmly, but one therapist becomes irritated and says: "You always think you know everything. That's why nobody likes working with you."
What began as a simple difference of opinion has now become a personal conflict.
The problem was not that the employees disagreed. The problem was how they handled the disagreement.
At Zura Spa, employees will not always have the same opinions, preferences or ideas. Differences may arise over schedules, responsibilities, instructions, work procedures and decisions.
Professionalism does not require everyone to agree. It requires everyone to remain respectful, even when they disagree.

sections.title: 2. What does courtesy mean?
paragraphs: Courtesy means treating other people with politeness, consideration and respect.
In the workplace, courtesy is demonstrated through the words we choose, the tone we use, our willingness to listen and the way we respond to other people's opinions.
Being courteous does not mean pretending to agree with something you believe is wrong.
It means expressing your position without unnecessary hostility, insults or humiliation.
Courtesy is not agreement. Courtesy is how we treat people while discussing our differences.

sections.title: Examples of courtesy
list: Listening without interrupting unnecessarily.
Speaking calmly, even when frustrated.
Avoiding insults and offensive language.
Asking questions before making assumptions.
Acknowledging another person's perspective.
Expressing disagreement respectfully.
Knowing when to pause a heated discussion.
Seeking clarification rather than immediately becoming defensive.

sections.title: 3. Why disagreements happen in the workplace
paragraphs: Disagreements are normal because employees have different experiences, personalities, responsibilities and perspectives.
A disagreement does not automatically mean someone is disrespectful or unwilling to cooperate.
The way people respond determines whether the disagreement becomes constructive or destructive.
table: Two therapists disagree about the most efficient preparation process
A receptionist gives an appointment update that a therapist misunderstands
Two employees disagree about who should replenish supplies
An employee believes duties are being distributed unfairly
A supervisor expects a task to be completed sooner than an employee anticipated
Colleagues prefer different approaches to organising shared spaces
An employee reacts sharply because she is frustrated or tired

sections.title: 4. Disagreement versus disrespect
paragraphs: The difference is simple: respectful disagreement addresses the issue; disrespectful disagreement attacks the person.
table: "You don't know what you're talking about."
"I have a concern about this approach."
"I understand your point, but I disagree."
"I think there may be a misunderstanding."
"I will make sure you regret this."

sections.title: 1. Listen before responding
paragraphs: Give the other person an opportunity to explain their position.
Do not assume you fully understand someone's point before they finish speaking.
Zura example: A therapist listens to the receptionist's explanation about an appointment change before responding.

sections.title: 2. Focus on the issue, not the person
paragraphs: Discuss the specific concern instead of attacking someone's character, intelligence or competence.
Instead of: "You are always careless."
Say: "The supplies were not ready before the appointment. How can we prevent this next time?"

sections.title: 3. Manage your tone
paragraphs: The way something is said can affect how it is received.
Avoid shouting, sarcasm, threatening language and deliberate humiliation.
A firm message can still be delivered politely.

sections.title: 4. Ask questions instead of making assumptions
paragraphs: When something seems wrong, seek clarification before accusing anyone.
Instead of: "You deliberately changed my schedule."
Say: "I noticed my schedule has changed. Could you explain the reason?"

sections.title: 5. Manage your emotions
paragraphs: Feeling upset is normal, but employees remain responsible for how they behave.
If you are becoming too frustrated to communicate constructively, request a short pause when appropriate.

sections.title: 6. Be willing to consider other perspectives
paragraphs: Your opinion may be reasonable without being the only reasonable opinion.
Consider whether another person's suggestion could improve the outcome.

sections.title: 7. Work toward a constructive outcome
paragraphs: The purpose of a workplace discussion should be to understand the issue, make a decision or find a solution.
Avoid turning every disagreement into a competition over who wins.

sections.title: 6. The difference between being firm and being rude
paragraphs: Some employees believe that speaking politely means being weak or allowing others to take advantage of them.
This is incorrect.
An employee can communicate firmly while remaining respectful.
Being courteous does not require you to abandon your position. It requires you to express it professionally.

items.label: Rude
items.body: "Stop disturbing me! Can't you see I'm busy?"

items.label: Firm and courteous
items.body: "I'm currently attending to a client. Please give me a few minutes, or contact the available staff member if it's urgent."

items.label: Rude
items.body: "I don't care what management says. I'm not doing it."

items.label: Firm and courteous
items.body: "I have concerns about this instruction. Could we discuss them before I proceed?"

sections.title: 7. How to disagree with colleagues
paragraphs: When you disagree with a colleague:
The second approach addresses the problem without creating an unnecessary personal conflict.
list: Choose an appropriate time and place for the discussion.
Explain your concern clearly.
Avoid embarrassing the person in front of clients or other employees.
Listen to their explanation.
Focus on facts and workplace standards.
Look for a reasonable solution.
Involve a supervisor if the issue cannot be resolved appropriately.

sections.title: Practical example — replenishing supplies
paragraphs: Two therapists disagree about who should replenish the supplies in a shared treatment room.
Unconstructive approach: "You're lazy. You always leave everything for me."
Constructive approach: "I noticed the supplies were not replenished after the last session. Can we clarify who is responsible so this doesn't happen again?"

sections.title: 8. How to disagree with supervisors and management
paragraphs: Employees may sometimes disagree with instructions, schedules, procedures or decisions.
Respecting authority does not mean employees must remain silent about genuine concerns.
However, concerns should be raised professionally.
If an instruction raises safety, harassment, legal or serious ethical concerns, employees should use the appropriate reporting or escalation process rather than feeling compelled to comply silently.

sections.title: A useful communication approach: Acknowledge → Explain → Suggest → Clarify

items.label: Explain
items.body: "I have a concern about the time required to complete it."

items.label: Suggest
items.body: "Would it be possible to adjust the sequence of the tasks?"

items.label: Clarify
items.body: "What would you prefer me to prioritise?"

sections.title: 9. What to do when a discussion becomes heated
paragraphs: Sometimes both people may begin to feel frustrated.
The goal should be to prevent the disagreement from becoming hostile.
Taking a pause can be a sign of emotional maturity rather than weakness.
For example: "I think we're both becoming frustrated. Can we take a short break and continue this discussion calmly?"

sections.title: Five practical steps
list: Recognise the signs. Notice raised voices, repeated interruptions, sarcasm or growing frustration.
Lower the intensity. Speak more calmly and avoid matching the other person's anger.
Pause if necessary. Suggest continuing the discussion after a short break, where appropriate.
Return to the actual issue. Avoid bringing unrelated past disagreements into the conversation.
Seek appropriate support. Involve a supervisor or manager if the issue cannot be resolved respectfully or safely.

sections.title: 10. Common mistakes during disagreements
table: Allow the other person to finish
Seek understanding and a practical resolution

sections.title: Case study A: The appointment disagreement
paragraphs: A receptionist informs a therapist that a client has requested an earlier appointment.
The therapist believes the change is unrealistic because she needs time to prepare the room.
The receptionist believes the appointment can be accommodated.
The discussion becomes tense.
Expected lesson: Both employees should focus on scheduling capacity, preparation requirements and the client's experience rather than attacking each other.
list: What is the actual issue?
How should the therapist express her concern?
How should the receptionist respond?
What information is needed to make a decision?
When should a supervisor become involved?

sections.title: Case study B: The supervisor's correction
paragraphs: A supervisor tells a therapist that her treatment room was not properly prepared.
The therapist believes she followed the required procedure.
She becomes upset and says: "You are always looking for something wrong with my work."
Expected lesson: Feedback should be specific and professional, and employees should be able to seek clarification without hostility.
list: Why might this response make the disagreement worse?
What questions could the therapist ask?
How should the supervisor explain the correction?
How can both people resolve the issue respectfully?

sections.title: Case study C: The unfair schedule
paragraphs: An employee believes her assigned shifts are less favourable than those of her colleagues.
She becomes angry and complains loudly during a staff meeting.
Expected lesson: Employees can challenge decisions respectfully, and management should respond fairly and professionally.
list: Is it wrong for the employee to raise a concern about fairness?
What was inappropriate about the way she communicated?
How could she raise the issue more effectively?
What responsibility does management have to consider legitimate concerns?

sections.title: Case study D: The personal insult
paragraphs: Two employees disagree about cleaning responsibilities.
One says: "You're so lazy. That's why nobody likes working with you."
Expected lesson: Workplace disagreements should focus on responsibilities and solutions, not personal humiliation.
list: What changed the disagreement into a personal attack?
How should the employee have expressed the concern?
What should the other employee do if the insults continue?
How can the team prevent similar conflicts?

sections.title: 12. Interactive exercise: Choose the courteous response
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 4 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: A colleague disagrees with your suggestion during a staff meeting. Tell her she doesn't know what she's talking about / Ask her to explain her perspective and discuss the options / Refuse to speak to her afterward
Your supervisor gives an instruction you believe is unclear. Ask politely for clarification / Ignore the instruction without explanation / Complain to colleagues that the supervisor is incompetent
A coworker speaks sharply to you because she is frustrated. Respond with an insult / Spread the incident around the workplace / Remain calm, set a respectful boundary and escalate if necessary
You realise your suggestion was not the best option. Continue arguing to protect your pride / Acknowledge the better option and cooperate / Blame someone else for the discussion
A disagreement becomes heated. Suggest a short pause and return to the issue calmly / Raise your voice to make yourself heard / Bring up unrelated past mistakes

sections.title: 13. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what it means to remain courteous during a disagreement.
Identify five behaviours that can turn a disagreement into a personal conflict.
Describe three ways to express disagreement respectfully.
Explain the difference between being firm and being rude.
How should you respond when you disagree with a supervisor's instruction?
Describe a workplace disagreement and explain how it could be resolved constructively, without naming individuals.
Identify three personal habits you will develop to improve how you handle disagreements.

sections.title: 14. Seven-day courtesy challenge
table: Listen fully before responding to a different opinion
Ask questions instead of making assumptions
Express a concern without personal criticism
Maintain a calm and respectful tone
Acknowledge a useful suggestion from a colleague
Practise pausing before responding when frustrated
Reflect on how you handled disagreements during the week

sections.title: 15. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Disagreements are a normal part of working with other people.
At Zura Spa, employees will sometimes have different opinions about schedules, responsibilities, procedures and decisions.
These differences do not have to damage relationships.
When employees listen carefully, speak respectfully, manage their emotions and focus on solutions, disagreements can become opportunities for improvement.
Courtesy should not disappear simply because someone disagrees with you.
Next topic: Separating Personal Feelings from Professional Responsibilities.

remember: You can disagree without being disrespectful. You can be firm without being rude. You can defend your position without attacking another person. Professional maturity is demonstrated not only by what you say, but also by how you say it—especially when you disagree.
